3|**Heliana’s Guide to Monster Hunting** is a third-party D&D supplement from **[[The Loot Tavern]]** that the Free League of Stickyickistan uses heavily for monster hunts, crafting, harvesting, unusual magic items, subclasses, spells, and weird creature-driven adventures.
4|
5|The book is built around the idea that monsters are not just obstacles. They are mysteries to investigate, dangerous encounters to survive, and valuable sources of materials if you know how to harvest them. A typical Heliana-style adventure might involve tracking a creature, learning its habits, preparing for its abilities, fighting it, then using parts of the monster to craft potions, gear, magic items, or other rewards.
6|
7|For players, this means:
8|
9|- Monster hunts may involve investigation, preparation, and research before combat.
10|- Creatures may have special traits, phases, weaknesses, or unusual rewards.
11|- Harvesting monster parts can matter.
12|- Crafting and alchemy may be more important than in a standard D&D game.
13|- Some species options, spells, items, and subclasses may come from Loot Tavern material.
14|- ==Always ask your DM== before assuming a Heliana option is available for your character.
15|
16|In the Free League, Heliana’s content is treated as part of the campaign’s extended toolbox. It fits Stickyickistan well because it supports strange monsters, magical biology, dangerous ingredients, and rewards that feel more interesting than just “you find gold.”
17|
18|## Links
19|
20|- [Heliana’s Guide to Monster Hunting]([https://www.dndbeyond.com/marketplace/sourcebooks/helias-guide-to-monster-hunting](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1))

25|

Copies have been found in Oeridian monster hunters’ lodges, Faerûnian wizard towers, Ansaloni taverns, noble Thranish libraries, Sigilite marketplaces, and the backpacks of people who absolutely should have read more than the first chapter before accepting a job.
27|
28|The book is advertised as an “extraplanar bestseller,” though no one is entirely sure which planes are included in the sales numbers. Different editions are known to contain contradictory marginal notes, suspicious stains, regional monster warnings, and occasional advice that seems to update itself after a reader survives something awful.
29|
30|Among adventurers, owning a copy is considered both practical and ominous. It usually means you are either preparing to hunt a monster, pretending to know how to hunt a monster, or about to become a cautionary sidebar in the next printing.
31|
32|#### ***Heliana’s Guide to Monster Hunting***
33|Wondrous Item, varies
34|
35|Full of useful knowledge and heavy enough to crush a skull, _Heliana’s Guide to Monster Hunting_ is nothing if not handy. The personalised quotes from [[Heliana]], [[Peeper]]’s deft proofing and editing, and the numerous ink stains and spilled watercolours give this hefty tome a homemade feel.
36|
37|**_Fantastic Phalanges and Where to Find Them._** As an action, you can open this book and stare intently at its pages, which turn of their own accord to settle on an anatomical diagram of the corpse nearest to the book. You immediately learn all the harvestable parts of the corpse, as well as their Component DCs.
38|
39|**_Know Thy Enemy._** As an action, you can place an object that belonged to a creature—such as its scat, scales, or clothing— between the pages of this book. One minute later, the book tells you a piece of information about the creature (number determined by rarity). At the GM’s discretion, this may be: its saving throw proficiencies, damage resistances, immunities, and vulnerabilities; condition immunities; creature’s type; one of its traits; or one of the clues acquired during a hunt. Placing more objects that belonged to that creature (or a creature with the same statblock) yields no further results.
40|
41|**_Weapon of the Learned._** This book can be used as a simple melee weapon that deals 1d6 bludgeoning damage on a hit. If you are proficient in [Arcana](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), [History](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), [Nature](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), or [Religion](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), you are proficient with this weapon.

A few useful design principles for **Heliana-style shops**:

1. **Every shop should care about different monster parts.**  
   A blacksmith wants bones, scales, shells, glands, and ores from monsters. An alchemist wants blood, venom, bile, spores, and organs. A cookhouse wants edible cuts, eggs, herbs, fats, and weird seasonings.

2. **Recipes should be social rewards.**  
   Don’t make every recipe buyable. Let shops teach rare recipes after the party proves themselves, brings rare materials, saves the business, or completes a contract.

3. **Monster parts should create complications.**  
   A part may rot, whisper, hatch, curse people, attract predators, violate local law, or be wanted by three different factions.

4. **Shops should drive hunts.**  
   A good shop is not just a place to spend gold. It should generate monster contracts, rumors, research leads, rival hunters, and crafting goals.

   - **Cookhouse:** monster meals, temporary buffs, cursed delicacies.

# Notes

## Pricing Notes

- Use normal item prices when convenient.
- Adjust monster-part value by rarity, danger, freshness, legality, and shop specialization.
- Shops should not buy every part at full value.
- The more specialized the shop, the better prices it offers for its preferred materials.
- Rare recipes should often be rewards, not simple purchases.

## Tone Notes

This shop should make monster hunting feel like an economy, not just a loot table. Every jar, hide, fang, organ, recipe, and contract should imply a creature, a story, or a problem waiting to happen.

# Jimmyjock Labingi

**Jimmyjock Labingi** was a legendary bard, poet, and early leader of the [[Twothirdlings]] of [[content/Regions/private/Doobius House|Doobius House]]. He is best remembered as a sharp-tongued champion of his mother’s people and one of the loudest voices against Elyrian settlement of his maternal ancestral lands.

## Background

Jimmyjock was the illegitimate son of [[Duke Doobius Highblade]] and a native concubine whose real name has been almost entirely erased from official records. Surviving Elyrian documents refer to her only as **“Mary Halfling-woman,”** a label that says more about the recordkeepers than it does about her.

Though Jimmyjock was raised with an unusual level of education for the time, Duke Doobius never truly accepted him as a legitimate son, largely because Jimmyjock was not fully human. Doobius later married a human woman, fathered human heirs, and left his estate to them when he died, leaving Jimmyjock with neither inheritance nor recognition.

## Rise to Leadership

Rather than seek acceptance from the family that rejected him, Jimmyjock turned toward his mother’s people. A gifted bard, poet, and speaker, he became known as a man of the people: educated enough to argue with nobles, angry enough to mock them in verse, and beloved enough that common folk repeated his songs long after officials tried to silence them.

When Duke Doobius finally died, the [[Twothirdlings]], who heavily outnumbered the Elyrian population around Doobius House, seized the moment. They claimed the estate and surrounding settlement as their own and elected Jimmyjock as their leader.

## Legacy

To the Twothirdlings, Jimmyjock Labingi is remembered as a folk hero: the disinherited son who chose his mother’s people over his father’s name. To Elyrian loyalists, he was a rebel, demagogue, and thief of noble property. Both versions agree on one thing: Jimmyjock knew exactly how to turn a song into a weapon.

## Traits

- **Role:** Legendary bard, poet, folk leader
- **Known For:** Anti-settler resistance, revolutionary songs, leadership of Doobius House
- **Personality:** Charismatic, defiant, witty, bitter toward noble hypocrisy
- **Ideal:** A people have the right to rule the land that remembers them.
- **Bond:** His erased mother and the Twothirdlings who claimed him as kin.
- **Flaw:** His hatred of Elyrian nobility could make compromise nearly impossible.

## Possible Sayings

> *“My father gave me no house, so my mother’s people gave me a homeland.”*

> *“A duke may own a deed. A people own the dirt beneath it.”*

> *“If they write your mother out of the records, sing her name louder.”*

# Molten Maw

**Molten Maw** is a colossal underground volcanic city in the [[Underdark]], inhabited mainly by [[Duergar]] and [[Svirfneblin]]. Built around a vast open caldera beneath the earth, the city serves as both a natural forge and a deadly hazard. Its streets are carved into black basalt terraces, iron gantries, cooled lava shelves, and tunnels reinforced against constant tremors.

Rivers of semi-intelligent, magically charged lava course through the city’s depths. Locals call these flows **the Red Veins**, and treat them less like ordinary magma and more like dangerous spirits of the earth. The lava sometimes changes course without warning, answers certain forms of elemental magic, or rises into half-formed elemental creatures that guard the flows from thieves, miners, and careless outsiders.

## Character

Molten Maw is brutal, smoky, rich, and paranoid. Every surface is warm. Every shadow glows faintly red. The air tastes of metal, ash, and old bargains. Duergar foundries hammer day and night, while Svirfneblin engineers maintain hidden vents, cooling chambers, pressure gates, and secret escape tunnels.

The city is famous for:

- Infernal heat and volcanic hazards
- Masterwork metal, obsidian, glass, and gemstone craft
- Hidden smuggler dens
- Elemental lava cults
- Political exiles and escaped criminals
- The underground black market known as [[The Silt Road]]

## The Silt Road

Criminals, rebels, fugitives, and desperate surface-folk sometimes flee to Molten Maw, surviving in fire-resistant cave networks and hidden market warrens. Over time, these routes became the heart of [[The Silt Road]], a literal underground criminal market that moves contraband, people, secrets, cursed goods, monster parts, and forbidden magic beneath the notice of surface authorities.

The Silt Road does not truly belong to any one faction. Duergar clans tax it, Svirfneblin guides navigate it, smugglers profit from it, and local gangs bleed for control of it.

## Notable Features

- **The Red Veins:** Semi-intelligent lava rivers that move through the city like living arteries.
- **The Chain Terraces:** Stacked residential districts connected by chains, lifts, bridges, and mine platforms.
- **The Cinder Warrens:** Smuggler caves, fugitive dens, and black-market stalls hidden behind cooling vents.
- **The Glass Forges:** Workshops where volcanic glass, enchanted slag, and fire-tempered gems are shaped.
- **The Ash Courts:** Harsh civic chambers where Duergar clan leaders, Svirfneblin engineers, and criminal brokers negotiate.
- **The Mouth Below:** A deeper volcanic pit believed to be either a planar wound, sleeping primordial, or the source of the Red Veins.

## Dangers

- Sudden lava surges
- Toxic gas pockets
- Collapsing tunnels
- Elemental guardians
- Duergar press gangs
- Svirfneblin sabotage traps
- Criminal ambushes
- Heat exhaustion
- Deals that are harder to escape than the city itself

- A fugitive the party needs has vanished into the Cinder Warrens.
- A shipment moving along [[The Silt Road]] contains something far worse than contraband.
- One of the Red Veins has begun spelling warnings in molten stone.
- A Duergar clan hires the party to recover a stolen forge-secret.
- A Svirfneblin engineer believes the Mouth Below is waking up.
- Surface rebels want weapons from Molten Maw, but buying them may empower the wrong faction.

[new]
# Upper South Booftown

## The Ashtray

**Upper South Booftown**, better known as **The Ashtray**, is where the streets are rough, the air is thick with soot, and the law only exists if someone nearby is willing to enforce it. Wedged between the slow-churning lava flows of [[Mount Zooka]] and the more “civilized” parts of the city, The Ashtray is a district of smoke-blackened rooftops, crooked tenements, ash-slick alleys, and hustlers who can smell weakness through a closed door.

The native [[Halflings|halfling]] population makes up a significant portion of the district’s residents, though The Ashtray is also home to outcasts, fugitives, dock toughs, failed apprentices, smugglers, off-duty mercenaries, and anyone else too useful, desperate, or dangerous to fit anywhere cleaner. It is not a safe neighborhood, but it is an honest one in its own crooked way: everyone knows what everything costs, even if the price is not always paid in coin.

## Character

The Ashtray feels like a city stacked on top of itself. Buildings climb over one another in a tangled mess of shoddy construction, patched bridges, rooftop walkways, hanging laundry lines, and half-legal expansions. The ground level belongs to carts, gangs, gamblers, and stray dogs. The upper levels belong to lookouts, rooftop gardens, hidden grow rooms, and people who do not want to be found.

The air is always warm and dirty. Ash from [[Mount Zooka]] settles on windowsills, food stalls, shrine steps, and sleeping children. Locals joke that if you leave a white shirt outside overnight, it wakes up as part of the neighborhood.

## Power on the Streets

The [[Mandem on Booftown]] (MOB) and the [[Cough City Crew]] (CCC) fight an endless turf war over illicit [[Arcannabis]] strains, underground fight rings, protection rackets, backroom gambling, bootlegged [[Alcohol]], and black-market [[Magitech]]. Their conflict is loud enough to terrify outsiders but familiar enough that residents know when to duck, when to run, and when to pretend they saw nothing.

Neither gang fully controls The Ashtray. Power shifts block by block, rooftop by rooftop, and business by business. A tea shop might pay MOB on Mondays, CCC on Fridays, and a local auntie every day because everyone knows she is the one actually keeping the street alive.

## Notable Features

- **The Sootsteps:** A maze of exterior stairs, ladders, rope bridges, and rooftop shortcuts used by locals to avoid gang checkpoints.
- **Cinder Courts:** Open lots where dice games, fistfights, public arguments, and informal trials are held.
- **Backroom Taverns:** Hidden drinking halls serving bootlegged [[Alcohol]], bad decisions, and worse information.
- **Ash Gardens:** Rooftop planters where locals grow hardy food, medicinal herbs, and discreet [[Arcannabis]] strains under layers of volcanic grit.
- **The Black Stalls:** A shifting night market for stolen goods, rare poisons, counterfeit papers, and illegal [[Magitech]] parts.
- **Smoke Chapels:** Tiny street shrines where residents pray for protection, revenge, luck, or a clean death.

## Reputation

Despite its lawless reputation, Upper South Booftown is not just a den of crime. It is a proving ground. Fortunes are made and lost in a single dice roll. Gangsters rule like kings until someone hungrier takes their corner. Bounty hunters stalk their marks through smog-choked streets, and even the smallest [[Halflings]] can rise to power if they are clever, ruthless, and loved by the right people.

To outsiders, The Ashtray is dangerous. To locals, it is home.

## Adventure Hooks

- A gang truce collapses after someone steals a rare Arcannabis strain from a rooftop grow.
- A bounty target is hiding in the Sootsteps, protected by locals who hate the person hunting them.
- A batch of black-market Magitech starts malfunctioning and setting buildings on fire.
- A respected halfling elder asks the party to remove a gang lieutenant without starting a district war.
- A child finds something valuable, cursed, or alive in a fresh fall of ash from [[Mount Zooka]].
- The MOB and CCC both want the same monster part, and neither side knows why the other wants it.
>>>>>>> END
</yolo_block>

Springwood is a MASSIVE naturalized park in the middle [[Stickyickistan]]. Even the [[Human Colonialism]] settlers knew these woods were too sacred to defile.

The Springwood is a broad, temperate forest filled with deciduous trees that existed in a state of perpetual spring, and dotted with a handful of human and gnomish settlements. [[Kerning’s Crossing]] lies along the region’s main trade route. # N.E.R.D

**N.E.R.D**, short for **Nerds Enjoy Researching Data**, is an arcane educational institution in [[Stickyickistan]] dedicated to magical research, mathematical theory, glyphwork, history, planar studies, and experimental problem-solving.

The institution is known for producing brilliant scholars, eccentric mages, obsessive researchers, and the occasional overconfident disaster. Its halls are filled with lecture chambers, enchanted chalkboards, sealed archives, unstable student projects, and libraries containing books that probably should not be available to first-year students.

## Role in Stickyickistan

N.E.R.D serves as one of [[Stickyickistan|Stickyickistan’s]] major centers of arcane education and magical research. Its professors and students are often consulted by city officials, adventuring parties, merchants, and private patrons when a problem requires brains, spells, obscure citations, or dangerous fieldwork.

The institution maintains an uneasy relationship with practical power. It claims to pursue knowledge for its own sake, but its research is valuable to nobles, guilds, inventors, monster hunters, and political factions across the region.

## Areas of Study

- Glyph-based magic
- Arcane mathematics
- History and archaeology
- Planar studies
- Exoterosology
- Magical engineering
- [[Magitech]]
- Monster research
- Alchemy

- Experimental enchantment

messages.content:
The **third shrine-box** on the Sootsteps is an old neighborhood offering shrine, not an official temple. It predates most of the newer tenements around it and likely began as a small urban shrine to [[The Three Sisters]], the old halfling nature goddesses of pre-colonization [[Stickyickistan]]. Its three rusted compartments once represented the Sisters: one for [[Ashalla]] and prayers for family, food, and safety; one for [[Darana]] and pleas for balance, fair weather, and clean dealings; and one for [[Shadash]] and the ugly prayers people only make when they have been wronged. In [[Upper South Booftown]], where ash, hunger, gang law, and bad luck all mingle together, the third box is the one people still use most.

Locals do not call it a shrine to Shadash too loudly, especially around followers of [[The Faith of the Sacred Flame]], but everyone knows what the third box is for. People leave burnt incense, copper bits, cheap liquor, ash-marked flowers, poison thorns, and folded notes naming debts, betrayals, illnesses, or enemies. Some ask Shadash to take their pain away. Others ask her to pass it along to someone who deserves it more. That makes it a perfect dead drop for the [[Ashen Shadow Society]]: sacred enough that most locals avoid disturbing it, feared enough that strangers hesitate to pry, and bitter enough that a black envelope hidden beneath the offering tray feels less like a crime and more like just another unanswered prayer.

  - **Respect the stinger.** A wyvern’s tail has longer reach than its bite and delivers a painful poison that can quickly turn a fair fight ugly.
  - **Do not let it carry anyone off.** Wyverns often weaken prey, seize it, and drag or fly it back to a cavernous lair to eat later.
- The contract comes with instructions for the Rite of Mind-Corpse Convergence.
- The Mind Blade was created by a mind flayer and can be carried by the party, but only its intended mind flayer or one of that mind flayer’s thralls can attune to it or use its magical properties.
- In any other creature’s hands, it functions as a normal sword of its kind.
- The rite starts by plunging the Mind Blade into the heart of a wyvern before its magical essence fades.
- The ritual requires continuous physical contact with the corpse or blade for 10 minutes, followed by a DC 15 Arcana check while the rite is incanted from the instructions.
- On a successful check, the Mind Blade is destroyed and the corpse transforms into a [[Bicephal Wyrmhole]] over 1 minute.
- If done correctly, the Mind Blade will be consumed by the Wyrmhole.
- The Society’s primary harvest target is the Wyrmhole’s claws; additional organs, residues, or magical materials are optional bonuses.
- The Society imposes a formal time limit of 3 days to completion before they start offering the contract to other monster hunters.

      "content": "15|## [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#Mechanics)Mechanics
16|
17|This section outlines how you, as the GM, can modify parameters to set the difficulty of the tracking experience, and how the players decide which checks they will make. These mechanics are designed to encourage your players to think creatively in how they use their characters’ skills, to encourage roleplay, and to flesh out exploration with interesting encounters. Any ability check made to find a monster, location, or to traverse terrain is referred to herein as a ‘Tracking check’.
18|
19|### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#SettingTrackingChecks)Setting Tracking Checks
20|
21|Before the players get rolling, you must set two parameters:
22|
23|- The minimum number of Tracking checks the party must make.
24|- The number of Tracking checks on which the party must succeed.
25|
26|The party must meet both of these conditions to find their destination. Increasing either of these parameters increases the difficulty of the tracking experience. The minimum number of checks represents a combination of the distance the party has to traverse and the density of possible encounters; a greater distance or a more populated area requires more checks. The number of successes represents how difficult it is for a creature or location to be found, or for terrain to be safely traversed. The minimum number of checks can never be less than the number of successes required.
27|
28|#### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#DeterminingChecksandSuccesses)Determining Checks and Successes
29|
30|You can determine how many Tracking checks a journey requires in the following way.
31|
32|**_Step 1: Areas._** Separate the journey into related areas. For example, if your party must cross grasslands to reach a swamp and then search that swamp for a monster, you can make grasslands one area, and the swamp another.
33|
34|**_Step 2: Encounter Chance._** Determine how likely encounters are to occur in each area. Encounters include both interesting environmental features and the presence of friendly or unfriendly creatures. Assign a number of Tracking checks to each area (minimum 1), with 1 representing a very low chance of an encounter and 5 extremely frequent encounters.
35|
36|**_Step 3: Successes._** Assign a number of Tracking successes (minimum 0) required to reach the next destination. A destination can be anything: the next area (for example, the swamp beyond the grassland), a city, or a monster’s lair. A large, obvious target, like a swamp, might require 0 successes, while a well-hidden location can require up to 3. You can use the table below to help determine an appropriate number of checks.
37|
38|#### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#SuggestedNumberofTrackingSuccesses)Suggested Number of Tracking Successes
39||Destination|Number of Successes|
40||---|---|
41||Obvious (e.g., huge waterfall)|0|
42||Natural (e.g., wolf den)|1|
43||Obscured (e.g., dragon’s lair)|2|
44||Protected (e.g., illusionist’s tower)|3|
45|
46|**_Duration._** A Tracking check can encapsulate any period of time from a minute to a month and is up to the GM to interpret. The more encounters the GM envisions the party experiencing in a given time, the shorter the duration each check should take. Sequential Tracking checks can even take different amounts of time from one another.
47|
48|For example, in a vast and open expanse, such as crossing a desert bereft of life, a single Tracking check might represent 30 days’ travel. In a particularly hostile environment, such as an ancient battlefield filled with undead, encounters might occur frequently and each Tracking check might represent 1 hour of searching. In a densely packed urban chase scene, a single Tracking check might take only 1 minute!
49|
50|GM Tip: Encounter Density
51|
52|If a Tracking check takes less than 8 hours, it is possible that the party can have more than one hostile encounter between long rests. As the hostile encounters are balanced to be very deadly, you should consider running them one or more levels lower than your average party level (APL).
53|
54|### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#MakingTrackingChecks)Making Tracking Checks
55|
56|This part of the tracking mechanics throws the narrative element of the game back to your players (which can be a fun dynamic shift!). You ask them how they’re approaching the tracking process and work with them to choose an ability and skill (or tool) for the Tracking check. Then you decide an appropriate DC for the check based on how likely the player’s proposition is to succeed. Finally, the player(s) make an ability check against the DC you’ve determined.
57|
58|Non-Standard Ability Checks
59|
60|You can mix and match skills/tools and abilities. For example, [Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills) is usually a Strength check. However, if a character states that they chase a wolf pack across 10 miles of snowy terrain, you might ask for a **Constitution ([Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))** check. All this requires the player to do is make a Constitution check and, if they have proficiency in Athletics, add their proficiency bonus to the result.
61|
62|When checks in this book use the word ‘or’, this indicates either skill/tool or ability can be used in any combination. For example, **Strength or Charisma ([Intimidation](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))** means the player can choose to make either a Strength or Charisma check and, if they have proficiency in the Intimidation skill, add their proficiency bonus. A **Strength or Dexterity ([Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills) or woodcarver’s tools)** check means you can use any one of the four check permutations: Strength ([Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills)), Dexterity ([Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills)), Strength (woodcarver’s tools), or Dexterity (woodcarver’s tools).
63|
64|#### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#Consequences)Consequences
65|
66|Success or failure, it enriches your world if you narrate the result of the party’s actions. On a success, you can simply narrate the changing landscape, or you can give the party a narrative encounter. These are non-combat encounters that can describe unique locations, non-hostile NPCs, or simply illustrate a remarkable environmental occurrence. Each biome contains a narrative encounter table; roll a **d8** and consult the relevant table for a plug and play idea!
67|
68|On a failure, the party has a hostile encounter. Each biome has a hostile encounter table; roll a **d4**, add the party’s ‘tier’ to the result, and consult the table to see who or what the party encounters!
69|
70||APL|Party’s Tier|
71||---|---|
72||1–4|1|
73||5–10|2|
74||11–16|3|
75||17–20|4|
76|
77|If the party meets both requirements of tracking (minimum checks and required successes), the party subsequently reaches the target they are tracking.
78|
79|**_Optional Rule: Critical Failure._** It’s possible for trackers to be given a false scent by a particularly devious enemy, or simply to royally mess up. In these cases, the tracking experience gets more difficult. A natural 1 on the d20, or missing the Tracking check DC by 10 or more, is a critical failure. Critically failing a Tracking check increases both the minimum number of checks and successes required to reach the destination by one.
80|
81|**_Optional Rule: Critical Success._** Sometimes, an especially observant or lucky tracker might find a clue allowing the party to find a lair more quickly. Surpassing the DC by 10 or more is a critical success and can count as two successes, while surpassing it by 20 or more counts as three successes. Perhaps your tracker, who, with the help of expertise and [guidance](https://www.dndbeyond.com/spells/2132-guidance), gets a 35 on their **DC 15 Wisdom ([Perception](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))** check, finds the imprint of a dropped stone tablet in the mud that details the exact way to disable the necromancer’s illusory protection, which counts as two additional successes.
82|
83|### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#ExampleDCs)Example DCs
84|
85|This list, which isn’t exhaustive, acts as guidance for deciding a Tracking check’s DC, with suggested abilities and skills to match. The DCs are balanced for mid-level characters; feel free to modify them as you see fit. For example, you might increase the DCs by 2 for characters of 12th level or higher, or decrease them by 2 for characters of 4th level or lower. In general, the more likely a character’s attempt is to succeed and the easier the circumstances affecting that check, the lower the DC.
86|
87|**_Common Sense Checks (DC 6)._** These checks are easily achievable by the common person.
88|
89|- Pursuing the footprints of a giant across mud—**Wisdom ([Survival](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
90|- Following a literal trail of breadcrumbs—**Wisdom ([Perception](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
91|- Using a compass to walk North—**Intelligence ([Nature](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
92|
93|**_Skilled Checks (DC 11)._** These checks are achievable by someone that has undergone basic training, such as a woodsman or acolyte.
94|
95|- Following the trail of a wolf through a forest—**Wisdom ([Survival](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
96|- Estimating the likely location of a creature based on its nature—**Intelligence** ([Arcana](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), [Nature](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), or [Religion](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills), depending on the creature’s type).
97|- Speaking with local animals to gain information—**Wisdom ([Animal Handling](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))** and the [speak with animals](https://www.dndbeyond.com/spells/2258-speak-with-animals) spell.
98|
99|**_Expert Checks (DC 16)._** These checks are beyond the skills of a trained commoner. Individuals able to regularly succeed on such checks have dedicated their life to mastery of a skill, such as a big-game hunter, professor of zoology, or [archmage](https://www.dndbeyond.com/monsters/16789-archmage).
100|
101|- Following a wolf’s trail across bare rock or after a snowstorm—**Wisdom ([Survival](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
102|- Mimicking a creature’s call to provoke a response from it—**Charisma ([Performance](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
103|- Climbing a tree to look for clues in the distance—**Dexterity or Wisdom ([Acrobatics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills) or [Perception](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
104|- Pushing oneself to explore a vast area in a short time—**Constitution ([Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
105|
106|**_Outlandish Checks (DC 21+)._** _“There’s always a chance this could work, right?”_ These checks often involve a degree of luck. The more outlandish, the more luck required, and the higher the DC.
107|
108|- Following a flying creature’s trail based on finding its kills and scat—**Wisdom ([Survival](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
109|- Making a canoe to more quickly navigate a water body—**Dexterity (woodcarver’s tools)**.
110|- Using brute force to smash through a cave wall and find a hidden tunnel—**Strength ([Athletics](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
111|- Consulting the stars to discern clues—**Intelligence or Wisdom ([Religion](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))**.
112|
113|**_Optional Rule: Varied Checks._** To keep things from getting stale, players can’t repeat the same Tracking check ability and skill/tool combination until two others have been attempted.
114|
115|### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#VariableDCsandModifiers)Variable DCs & Modifiers
116|
117|The random encounter descriptions use the abbreviations **APL** (average party level), **VDC** (variable difficulty class), **Vmod** (variable modifier), and **Vdam** (variable damage). Using these variable statistics allows the same encounter to be challenging for every party by scaling the difficulty of certain interactions with APL. In some cases, modifiers may be placed on these variable statistics, like “the player character takes cold damage equal to twice the **Vdam**” or “the creature has a **Dexterity ([Stealth](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/free-rules/playing-the-game#Skills))** modifier of **Vmod+5**”. For a party of 3rd level, this latter example would yield a total modifier of **+9**.
118|
119|#### [](https://www.dndbeyond.com/sources/dnd/hgtmh1/tracking#VariableStatisticsSummary)Variable Statistics Summary
120||APL|VDC|Vmod|Vdam|
121||---|---|---|---|
122||1-2|11|+3|2 (**1d4**)|
123||3-4|12|+4|3 (**1d6**)|
124||5-6|13|+5|5 (**2d4**)|
125||7-8|14|+6|7 (**2d6**)|
126||9-11|15|+7|10 (**3d6**)|
127||12-14|16|+8|14 (**4d6**)|
128||15-17|17|+9|21 (**6d6**)|
129||18-20|18|+10|28 (**8d6**)|
130|"
    }

189|The DM may replace these options with another region of [[The Outback]] or a location appropriate to the campaign.
190|
191|## Tracking the Wyvern
192|
193|For a time save, the DM can omit the tracking stage and begin the adventure with the party arriving at the wyvern’s hunting grounds. The Society may provide a map, instructions, or a guide. If the tracking stage is played, use the following procedure.
194|
195|### Setting the Tracking Challenge
196|
197|Before the party begins, decide how many Tracking checks are required and how many successes are needed to reach the wyvern’s lair. The party must meet both requirements. For this adventure, use **four Tracking checks and two successes**. The checks represent travel through the selected environment, while the successes represent locating the wyvern’s hidden lair.
198|
199|Separate the journey into relevant areas. For example, a mountain hunt might include the approach road, the lower slopes, and the wyvern’s nesting cavern. Before the party begins, decide how many Tracking checks are required and how many successes are needed to reach the wyvern’s lair. The party must meet both requirements. For this adventure, use **four Tracking checks and two successes**. The checks represent travel through the selected environment, while the successes represent locating the wyvern’s hidden lair.

Separate the journey into relevant areas. For example, a mountain hunt might include the approach road, the lower slopes, and the wyvern’s nesting cavern. Assign at least one Tracking check to each area. A failed check creates a hostile encounter; a successful check creates a narrative encounter or no encounter, at the DM’s discretion. Continue making checks until the party has completed at least four checks and achieved at least two successes.

A natural 1 or a failure by 10 or more is a critical failure. Increase the required number of checks and successes by 1. Be cautious with this rule in a one-shot, since repeated failures can extend the adventure significantly. Surpassing the DC by 10 or more counts as two successes; surpassing it by 20 or more counts as three successes.
value.newText:
Use **three Tracking checks and two required successes**. The party must make all three checks, but they only need two successes to locate the wyvern on favorable terms. This keeps tracking meaningful without letting it consume the whole session.

Divide the hunt into three quick areas:

| Check | Area | What It Represents |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | The approach trail | Reaching the marked territory and spotting signs of wyvern activity |
| 2 | The feeding grounds | Reading kills, droppings, drag marks, broken branches, or frightened wildlife |
| 3 | The nesting cliffs | Finding the active lair or choosing a safer place to draw the wyvern out |

A success gives the party useful information, a better approach, or a chance to prepare. A failure still moves the hunt forward, but causes a complication. Do not add extra required checks for critical failures in this one-shot. Instead, a natural 1 or failure by 10 or more gives the wyvern **1 Hunt Advantage**.

Surpassing the DC by 10 or more counts as two successes. If the party reaches two successes before the third check, still run the final check, but use it to determine whether they gain an extra advantage before the fight.

On a successful check, describe the changing landscape and give the party one useful benefit. On a failed check, the party still progresses, but the wyvern or the environment gains leverage. Avoid adding full extra combats unless you have time; use complications, hazards, and foreshadowing instead.

Track the party’s total successes and the wyvern’s **Hunt Advantage**.

## Tracking Outcomes

| Result After 3 Checks | Outcome |
|---|---|
| 3+ successes | The party finds the wyvern before it spots them. They may choose the battlefield, set bait, hide, or prepare for 10 minutes before initiative. |
| 2 successes | The party locates the active nesting cliffs normally. Neither side has a major advantage. |
| 0–1 successes | The party reaches the lair, but the wyvern has noticed them. It begins hidden or airborne, and the DM should start the encounter with the wyvern in a favorable position. |

## Hunt Advantage

The wyvern gains **1 Hunt Advantage** whenever the party critically fails a Tracking check, makes excessive noise, leaves obvious bait unattended, or spends too long resting in its territory.

Spend Hunt Advantage during the wyvern encounter as follows:

| Hunt Advantage | Effect |
|---:|---|
| 1 | The wyvern starts airborne instead of perched or grounded. |
| 2 | The wyvern has already circled the party; it begins combat with cover, concealment, or an unexpected angle of attack. |
| 3+ | The wyvern attempts to isolate a vulnerable target before initiative, such as a mount, hireling, familiar, or separated character. |

## Quick Success Benefits

When a character succeeds on a Tracking check, choose or roll one benefit.

| d4 | Benefit |
|---:|---|
| 1 | The party identifies a safe approach and avoids loose scree, thin ledges, or a dangerous climb. |
| 2 | The party finds evidence of the wyvern’s feeding pattern and knows it prefers strafing attacks before landing. |
| 3 | The party discovers old remains from past victims; they can salvage a minor useful item or clue. |
| 4 | The party spots a wind-sheltered ambush site, giving them a good place to hide, set bait, or prepare.

messages.content:
You’re right — “2 required successes” was awkward if we’re also saying there are only ever 3 fixed checks and no extra checks. I cleaned that up.

I updated the tracking structure to:

- **3 fixed Tracking checks**
- No extra checks added for failures
- Each success gives useful information / positioning / preparation
- Each failure causes a **1d4 Tracking Complication**
- Critical failures still give the wyvern **1 Hunt Advantage**
- Big successes grant an extra benefit instead of shortening the stage

I also added this complication table:

```markdown
## Tracking Complications

When the party fails a Tracking check, roll or choose one complication. These should cost time, resources, positioning, or safety without turning into a full extra combat.

| d4 | Complication |
|---:|---|
| 1 | **Bad Ground.** Loose scree, a thin ledge, or a sudden rockslide forces the party into a risky crossing. Each character must succeed on a DC 13 Dexterity saving throw or take minor bludgeoning damage and start the wyvern encounter without ideal footing. |
| 2 | **Poisoned Kill Site.** The party finds a half-eaten carcass tainted by wyvern venom. A character inspecting it too closely must succeed on a DC 13 Constitution saving throw or suffer mild poison symptoms until the next short rest. |
| 3 | **False Nest.** The party follows signs to an abandoned nest littered with bones and stolen junk. They lose time, and the wyvern gains 1 Hunt Advantage unless the party immediately changes tactics. |
| 4 | **Shadow Overhead.** The wyvern passes somewhere above the clouds or cliff line. The party catches only a glimpse, but it may have caught their scent. The next Tracking check is made with disadvantage unless the party hides, masks their scent, or waits for better cover. |
```

And I revised the outcomes to count total successes after 3 checks:

```markdown
| Result After 3 Checks | Outcome |
|---|---|
| 3 successes | The party reads the hunt perfectly. They find the wyvern before it spots them and may choose the battlefield, set bait, hide, or prepare for 10 minutes before initiative. |
| 2 successes | The party handles the hunt well. They locate the active nesting cliffs normally, and neither side has a major advantage unless Hunt Advantage says otherwise. |
| 1 success | The party finds the wyvern, but their approach is messy. The wyvern starts alert, suspicious, or already airborne. |
| 0 successes | The party reaches the lair the hard way. The wyvern has definitely noticed them and begins the encounter in a favorable position. |
```

This should make the tracking stage feel more like a **scorecard** than a pass/fail gate.

messages.content:
For this adventure, I’d make each tracking check represent **about 1 hour**, with the whole tracking stage taking **roughly 3 hours in-world**.

That keeps it meaningful without turning the hunt into a full travel day.

Suggested breakdown:

| Check | Area | Time Represented | Why |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 1 | The approach trail | 1 hour | Reaching the marked territory, checking old signs, getting oriented |
| 2 | The feeding grounds | 1 hour | Studying kills, droppings, drag marks, broken trees, scattered bones |
| 3 | The nesting cliffs | 1 hour | Climbing, scouting ledges, finding the active nest or baiting the wyvern |

I’d phrase it in the adventure like this:

```markdown
Each Tracking check represents about **1 hour** of careful travel, searching, scouting, and interpreting signs. The full tracking stage usually takes **3 hours in-world**, plus any extra time the party spends resting, setting bait, casting rituals, or preparing an ambush.
```

If you want failures to matter without adding more checks, you can tie time to complications:

```markdown
A failed Tracking check still moves the party forward, but the complication usually costs resources, worsens positioning, or adds **1 extra hour** to the hunt.
```

So the simple rule would be:

- **Normal tracking stage:** 3 hours
- **Each failed check:** +1 hour
- **Critical failure:** +1 hour and the wyvern gains **1 Hunt Advantage**
- **Party stops for a short rest / elaborate ambush prep:** add that time normally

This creates a nice pressure point because the Society gave them a **3-day limit**, but the more immediate danger is that lingering in wyvern territory gives the creature more chances to notice them.

The wyvern’s lair contains bones, torn hides, scraps of equipment, and the remains of previous prey. The creature has chosen a defensible position with a clear flight path and narrow approaches.

When the characters enter the lair, the wyvern regains 2d10 hit points. It fights to the death because the characters threaten its home, territory, and food supply.

Possible lair hazards include:

- Unstable ledges or loose stone.
- Deep shafts and sudden drops.
- Difficult terrain caused by bones and debris.
- Narrow passages that limit flight.
- Wind, smoke, steam, or volcanic heat.
- Food stores that attract scavengers during the battle.
value.newText:
## Wyvern Lair

The wyvern’s lair is a high cavern, cliffside hollow, or ruined watchpost with a wide opening large enough for the creature to fly through. It has chosen the site for visibility, vertical space, and easy escape routes rather than comfort. The floor is littered with bones, torn hides, splintered carts, broken tack, cracked chests, scraps of armor, and the remains of previous prey dragged here to be eaten in safety.

The lair should make the wyvern feel like an aerial ambusher, not a dragon defending a treasure hoard. It uses ledges, ceiling height, wind, and narrow approaches to stay mobile while forcing the characters to deal with bad footing and exposed positions. Most wyverns do not hoard treasure intentionally, but useful loot may be mixed into the debris from victims, livestock caravans, small boats, or wagons carried off with prey.

When the characters enter the lair, the wyvern may regain **2d10 hit points** if it had time to retreat, settle, and recover. It fights more aggressively here, but it is still an animalistic opportunist. It defends its food, territory, and escape route, but it does not need to fight to the death if an obvious way out remains. If reduced to low hit points and given a clear flight path, it may try to flee deeper into the mountains unless the characters corner it or force the final confrontation.

Possible lair hazards include:

- **High ledges.** The wyvern perches above the party and drops onto exposed targets.
- **Deep shafts and sudden drops.** A shoved, grappled, or careless creature risks falling.
- **Loose stone and unstable scree.** Fast movement may trigger slides or difficult terrain.
- **Bone piles and prey debris.** The ground is difficult terrain and may hide useful salvage.
- **Narrow approaches.** The party may have to enter single file while the wyvern has room to fly.
- **Crosswinds, smoke, steam, or volcanic heat.** Ranged attacks and flight may be complicated by the terrain.
- **Trapped food stores.** Half-dead prey, scavengers, or venom-tainted carcasses may distract or endanger the party.
